attempts.entry_title: Chandelier-cell temporal gating and L5 bursting in mouse V1 (Jarzebowski & Bendor 2026)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings hold up in this data and in a rebuild of its model. In the recordings, L2/3 and L5 bursting is highest on the first repetition of an image and running raises it, as reported. Omission firing and L5 bursting fall below spontaneous levels only in part, depending on which spontaneous period is used, which the Methods leave open; running did not lower L5 firing during omissions. In the model, the prediction did not silence the neuron under weak sensory input and gain changed the release delay, probably because the model's code and input timings are not available. Two supplementary findings, on novel images and on L5 bursting and rate, did not reproduce.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Jarzebowski and Bendor (2026) on dandiset 000713, the Allen Institute's Visual Behavior Neuropixels recordings, which the paper reuses. It simulates the paper's two-compartment model of an L2/3 neuron from its Methods, and on the recordings selects putative pyramidal, image-responsive L2/3 and L5 units of VISp (layer from the CCFv3 annotation) and tests how their bursting and firing change with image repetition, omission, novelty and running.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Jarzebowski & Bendor (2026) from dandiset 000713 and the paper's model

outcomes.statement: In the two-compartment model, L4 sensory input without L5 IT predictive input makes the L2/3 neuron fire a short-latency singlet or doublet, depending on L4 strength, immediately after the input arrives; basket cell inhibition ends the response.
outcomes.source: Results, Positive prediction error, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: When L4 sensory input arrives in the absence of L5 IT predictive input, the L2/3 neuron produces a singlet or doublet depending on the L4 input strength ... Because no ChC clamp is active, action potential initiation at the AIS is rapid and unimpeded. The resulting spike or burst occurs immediately following sensory input arrival
outcomes.notes: With L4 at 60 nS and no prediction all 80 runs spike, first spike a median 3.75 ms after L4 onset; half the runs fire doublets from 90 nS and all from 115 nS. Under the claim's seed 1 of 81 spikes at 60 nS (0.012) falls after the basket conductance peak (8.5 ms after L4 onset), so the strict "no spike after the basket peak" fails; seeds plus 1000 to 4000 give latencies 3.7 to 3.8 ms and 0 or 0.012 late spikes (criterion met under 3 of 5). Over every L4 from 0 to 150 nS, 0.009 of first spikes and 0.046 of all spikes fall after the basket peak under the claim's seed: single spikes at weak L4 (15 to 30 nS, 18 spikes), second spikes of doublets (75 to 120 nS, 119 spikes) and 1 each at 60, 65 and 70 nS.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
The criterion's first few ms is read as before the basket conductance peak (8.5 ms), a choice made here.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in full in the Methods (Brian 2); its code (github.com/bendor-lab/SETA-model_allen_analysis) was not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: With L5 IT predictive input and no sensory input, the ChC clamp holds the AIS below threshold and the neuron fires a single gated release spike after the clamp decays, 15 to 20 ms after the time the same L5 IT input could have triggered the L5 ET bAP.
outcomes.source: Results, Negative prediction error, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: In the absence of additional sensory drive from L4, the AIS cannot escape this clamp until ChC conductance sufficiently decays, at which point the accumulated depolarisation is released as a singlet if the soma remains sufficiently depolarised ( Fig. 1D ). In such case, the L2/3 input arrives to the L5 ET 15–20 ms delayed
outcomes.notes: L5 IT 12 nS and ChC 25 nS without L4, 80 runs. 97.5% of runs spike and all spiking runs fire one spike. Median latency from L5 IT onset (reading a) 17.4 ms, inside 13.5 to 22 ms; from the L5 IT peak (reading b) 9.4 ms, outside. Over the five seeds reading (a) gives 17.1 to 17.9 ms.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
The criterion names two readings of the reference time; the claim holds under reading (a) and not under (b).
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: When L4 input is weaker than the predictive input, the ChC clamp vetoes the L2/3 spike and basket cell inhibition prevents the gated release spike, so the neuron is silent.
outcomes.source: Results, The circuit encodes a continuous error spectrum, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: When L4 input was weaker than the predictive input, the ChC clamp successfully vetoed the L2/3 spike, and basket cell hyperpolarisation prevented the gated release spike ( Fig. 2A ), resulting in no spiking.
outcomes.notes: With L5 IT 12 nS, ChC 25 nS and L4 from 2 to 11.9 nS (basket 1.2 times L4, simultaneous onset), the expected count is 0.90 to 0.975 per run, against 0.975 for the prediction alone; the five seeds give 0.89 to 0.99. The neuron is quietest near L4 40 nS (0.15 spikes per run), where L4 conductance exceeds L5 IT's, so the paper's "weaker than the predictive input" may compare the inputs on another scale. Without noise the failure is the same: a release spike fires at 18.7 ms for every L4 from 0 to 10 nS and none from 12 nS. At L4 10 nS the basket conductance (1.2 times L4) peaks at 12 nS and has fallen to 6.4 nS at 18 ms while L5 IT is still 7.7 nS and ChC 4.5 nS, so the AIS reaches threshold as the clamp decays. In this model the release spike is vetoed only when L4 is at least as strong as L5 IT in conductance; a question to a reader asks how the paper compares the two inputs.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: A sufficiently strong L4 input during the active ChC clamp overrides it and drives a breakthrough spike, but the L4 conductance needed for a doublet is higher than without a prediction.
outcomes.source: Results, The circuit encodes a continuous error spectrum, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: When the L4 input was sufficiently strong and arrived during the active ChC clamp window, it overrode the clamp and drove a spike, a breakthrough event, albeit with a higher threshold for producing a doublet relative to a completely unpredicted positive error ( Fig. 2B ).
outcomes.notes: With prediction every run spikes at L4 150 nS and no L4 up to 150 nS gives a doublet under either reading; without it the doublet threshold is 110 nS (expected count 2, reading a) or 90 nS (half the runs, reading b). Searched to 600 nS, the thresholds with prediction are 345 and 260 nS. All five seeds agree (110 to 120 and 90 nS without prediction).
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
The threshold with prediction lies above the 0 to 150 nS plotting range; the range was extended to 600 nS to find it, which changes no comparison.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: Delaying either the predictive or the sensory input by 5 ms leaves the model's behaviour the same.
outcomes.source: Results, The circuit encodes a continuous error spectrum, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: The model was robust to exact time difference between prediction and sensory inputs and delaying either input by 5 ms resulted in the same behaviour ( Fig. 2C ).
outcomes.notes: At L4 60 nS with prediction the expected count is 0.775 at 0 ms delay, and differs by 0.225 when the prediction is delayed 5 ms and 0.3125 when the sensory input is, both below 0.5. Seeds give differences 0.125 to 0.3125.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
The L4 conductance of the Figure 2B arrow is not given; the Methods' default 60 nS is used, as the criterion says.

outcomes.statement: As sensory input weakens relative to the prediction, the latency of the breakthrough spike lengthens continuously.
outcomes.source: Results, The circuit encodes a continuous error spectrum, paragraph 1; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: As sensation weakened relative to prediction, breakthrough latency lengthened ... the resulting L2/3 spike arrived progressively later relative to the bAP ( Fig. 2D )
outcomes.notes: Over 31 L4 conductances (0 to 150 nS) where runs spike, the mean first-spike latency falls from 18.4 ms to 2.36 ms, Spearman rho -0.999. The largest 5 nS step, 3.25 ms between 35 and 40 nS, resampled at 1 nS with 4000 runs per conductance, changes latency by 3.03 ms in five steps of which the largest is 1.30 ms (0.43 of the change), and 0.40 of first spikes in that interval fall between 8 and 12 ms, between the release and breakthrough latencies. Seeds give rho -0.989 to -0.999 and a largest 1 nS share of 0.23 to 0.43. The coarse test against a quarter of the latency range fails under 3 of 5 seeds (steps of 5.25, 6.28 and 6.06 ms); the resampling shows these steps are sampling noise of the 80-run means.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.

Assumption. "Without a single jump" is tested as continuity, a choice made here as the criterion gives no number. The interval of the largest 5 nS step is resampled at 1 nS with 4000 runs; a jump is one 1 nS step that carries more than half the latency change across that interval. The earlier test (largest 5 nS step below half the latency range) and a stricter one (below a quarter) are printed.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: At low somatic gain of L4 and L5 IT, strong sensory input rarely drives bursts and an omission (prediction only) often ends in silence instead of a gated release spike.
outcomes.source: Results, Precision weighting of prediction error, paragraph 1; Figure 3A
outcomes.quote: At low gain, both error signals were effectively suppressed ... strong sensory inputs rarely drove bursts, and stimulus omission frequently ended in silence
outcomes.notes: High gain bursts from L4 115 nS (8 conductances up to 150 nS); at those, no Low-gain sensory run fires two spikes (fraction 0.0, High 1.0), and all Low-gain prediction-only runs are silent (1.0; Mid 0.9875, High 0.075). All five seeds agree.

outcomes.statement: Raising L4 and L5 IT gain lowers the sensory threshold for bursts and raises the probability of a gated release spike on omission trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Precision weighting of prediction error, paragraph 1; Figure 3A and 3B
outcomes.quote: As L4 and L5 IT gain increased the sensory threshold for bursts decreased (favouring LTP; Fig. 3A,B ), and the probability of a gated release spike on omission trials increased (favouring LTD; Fig. 3B ).
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b) the burst threshold falls from 515 nS (Low) to 230 (Mid) to 115 (High). With 800 prediction-only runs per gain the omission spike probability is 0.0, 0.026 and 0.948, so it rises from Low to Mid to High; all five seeds meet the criterion (Mid 0.013 to 0.040, Low 0 of 800 in every seed). With 80 runs, as in the first run, Mid gave 0.0 under the claim's seed and the strict rise failed; 80 runs cannot resolve a probability near 0.03. Under reading (a) no Low-gain threshold is found up to 600 nS and Mid and High are 350 and 355 nS, so (a) fails. Changed from partially reproduced after verification.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
Thresholds are searched over L4 0 to 600 nS (a plotting choice) so that one is found at each gain.
The omission probability is estimated from 800 runs per gain (80 elsewhere), a precision choice: the Mid-gain probability is about 0.03.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: Gain does not substantially change the delay of the gated release spike when it occurs.
outcomes.source: Results, Precision weighting of prediction error, paragraph 1; Figure 3C
outcomes.quote: Critically, increased gain did not substantially alter the delay of the gated release spike when it occurred ( Fig. 3C ).
outcomes.notes: Prediction only at gains 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0. No run spikes at Low gain, 1 of 80 at Mid (latency 24.0 ms) and 76 at High (median 17.35 ms), so a release delay exists at two gains, 6.65 ms apart, above the 5 ms the criterion allows. Seeds give 1 to 4 spiking Mid runs at 22.1 to 34.8 ms against 17.35 to 18.2 ms at High. The paper's "when it occurred" may refer to a regime where release spikes occur at every gain, which the Methods' parameters do not give. With 800 runs per gain, Low gain has no spiking run in any seed, Mid 18 to 24 runs at a median 22.6 to 26.2 ms and High 17.6 to 17.9 ms, 5.0 to 8.3 ms apart.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.

outcomes.source: Results, L4 excitatory drive / basket cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: Reducing basket cell conductance relative to L4 excitatory drive lowers the burst firing threshold ( Fig. 4A ).
outcomes.notes: Burst threshold (mean count >= 2, 10 runs) 55, 65, 85 and 105 nS at basket scalings 0.6, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2. All five seeds agree (1.2 gives 95 to 105 nS).
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.

outcomes.statement: Reducing ChC conductance shortens the latency of the first L2/3 spike for a given L4 strength and lowers the L4 needed for a positive error.
outcomes.source: Results, L5 IT excitatory drive / chandelier cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: Reducing chandelier cell conductance relative to L5 IT excitatory drive decreased L2/3 spike latency for a given L4 strength reducing the L4 threshold required for generating a positive error ( Fig. 4B ).
outcomes.notes: L5 IT 12 nS, ChC 0 to 50 nS, L4 0 to 150 nS, 10 runs. At all 16 L4 conductances where every ChC level has spiking runs, latency rises with ChC (rho 0.46 to 0.99, median 0.95). The breakthrough threshold rises with ChC from 0 to 115 nS (rho 0.97). Taken literally, the lowest L4 > 0 with expected count >= 0.5 is 5 nS at every ChC level, because the release spike fires at weak L4, so that part of the criterion cannot fall; the outcome rests on reading it as the breakthrough threshold. All five seeds agree. Question for the authors in the findings.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
ChC 0 to 50 nS in steps of 5 is a plotting choice.

Assumption. The lowest L4 that drives a spike is taken as the breakthrough threshold, the lowest L4 above the conductance of least firing where the expected count reaches 0.5, after the paper's 'L4 threshold required for generating a positive error' (Results, L5 IT excitatory drive / chandelier cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 1). The plain reading is printed and cannot decide the claim.
outcomes.where: the paper's two-compartment LIF model, specified in the Methods; code not public on 2026-11-21

outcomes.statement: Without sensory input, raising L5 IT conductance with ChC fixed at 25 nS shortens the release spike latency, and strong L5 IT input can produce a doublet instead of a singlet.
outcomes.source: Results, L5 IT excitatory drive / chandelier cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 1; Figure 4C and 4D
outcomes.quote: In the absence of sensory input, release-spike latency shortened with rising predictive drive ( Fig. 4C ), and for strong L5 IT inputs could produce a doublet
outcomes.notes: Without L4, median release latency falls from 17.1 ms at L5 IT 12 nS to 7.7 ms at 40 nS (rho -1.0), and the expected count reaches 2 at 22 nS. Seeds on a 12 to 120 nS grid give rho -0.9993 to -0.9996 and doublets from 24 nS.
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.

outcomes.statement: With strong L5 IT drive, weak sensory inputs reach the burst threshold at a lower L4 conductance.
outcomes.source: Results, L5 IT excitatory drive / chandelier cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 1; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: We also observed that weak sensory inputs interacting with strong L5 IT drive had a lower burst threshold ( Fig. 4D ).
outcomes.notes: ChC 25 nS; burst threshold 355, 360, 330, 0, 0 and 0 nS for L5 IT 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 and 32 nS (rho -0.88). From 24 nS L5 IT alone gives doublets, so the threshold is 0. Seeds give rho -0.88 to -0.94. Most of the fall comes from L5 IT alone: from 12 to 20 nS the threshold is 310 to 360 nS, rises from 12 to 16 nS under 2 of the 5 seeds, and is lower at 20 than at 12 nS under all five (by 15 to 40 nS).
deviations: The model is integrated in NumPy with the Euler-Maruyama method at dt 0.1 ms from the Methods' equations and parameters (Methods, Computational model of L2/3 neuron; Synaptic connectivity and kinetics), not in Brian 2, as the paper's code was not public; 50 ms of rest before the inputs and a 100 ms counting window are standard choices.
L5 IT 12 to 32 nS in steps of 4 and L4 up to 600 nS are plotting choices; the threshold at 12 nS lies above 150 nS.

outcomes.statement: Raising the ChC conductance, or lowering the ChC reversal potential, can restore the release spike latency after an increase in L5 IT drive.
outcomes.source: Results, L5 IT excitatory drive / chandelier cell inhibitory balance, paragraph 2; Figure 4E and 4F

With 10 runs a median within 1 ms can occur by chance on a fine grid.

findings.statement: In 7 sessions, 351 VISp units that pass the quality criteria have peak-channel CCF coordinates x, y and z all 0, while the electrodes table names their location VISp. The zeros stand for missing coordinates, so these units cannot be given a layer.

The units and electrodes tables have no column descriptions (firing_rate, waveform_duration, snr, isi_violations, presence_ratio, amplitude_cutoff, x, y, z among them). Units (Hz, ms, um in the CCF) can be read from the values and the Allen documentation, but not from the files.

In session 20211111T220915 the 10 s spontaneous block that in the other 152 sessions follows the active task by 18 to 29 s starts 3277 s after the last task presentation, and the later blocks follow correspondingly later. The files do not say what happened in the gap.

Checks that passed. 153 sessions from 81 mice, no two sharing a spike-train signature; 4795 to 4811 active-task presentation rows (with omissions) per session at 750 ms onset intervals; spontaneous blocks of 10.0 and 289.0 s; running speed in cm/s. The VISp population count separates images from omissions 30 to 100 ms after onset (median AUC 0.95) and not before onset (0.44 to 0.56), consistent with spikes and stimulus tables sharing a clock. In 10 sessions the AUC is below 0.8 (lowest 0.55, 20201203T231053), and 2 sessions have no VISp unit passing the criteria (20210616T205318, 20210819T204407); there the shared clock is not established here. 7996 of 7997 VISp units with coordinates fall in VISp in the CCFv3 annotation.

verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook of the run after the reader's answer (commit c69951d) with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper modules vbn.py and seta_model.py and the claims file, with the paper's text. The verifier checked the version through the DANDI API, tested the helpers on synthetic inputs (_counts, fsb, mod_index, run_state, alpha) and ran the model module with noise switched off. It had no attempt record.

disagreements.reason: Rho is -0.989 to -0.999, but the no-jump test uses the author's own threshold of half the latency range, which is lenient; the largest step is 2.8 to 6.3 ms of a 16 ms range, at the switch from release to breakthrough spikes (35 to 40 nS), and a quarter of the range would fail 3 of 5 seeds (problem 4).

Under reading (b) the burst threshold falls from 515 to 565, to 215 to 230, to 110 to 115 nS in all seeds, and omission spike probability is 0, then 0 to 0.075, then about 0.94. The strict rise from Low to Mid fails in 2 seeds because both are 0, but pooled over the 5 seeds it is 0/400 against 12/400; the per-seed tests rest on very few spiking runs (problem 9).

Using spontaneous block 3 or both blocks with O5 a, both layers are negative with p < 1e-8 but outside tolerance; with block 1, the reading the notebook adopts, L2/3 is not significant (p = 0.75 or 0.87). Block 1 (10 s, 40 windows, median 0 stationary windows) is adopted as the period immediately following the task, but block 1 starts 17.95 to 3276.62 s after the task and this was never investigated, and the Results' "spontaneous activity outside the stimulus blocks" allows block 3 (problem 2). O5 assumes a single block (problem 12).

With block 3 or both blocks, O5 a, the difference measure gives -0.0053 to -0.0071 (p of 0.02 to 0.03), outside the -0.004 to -0.001 tolerance; with block 1 the sign reverses (+0.007 to +0.008, p < 0.03). The block choice flips the sign (problem 2).

verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the revision after round 1 (as at commit a7d55e8), the helper modules, the claims file, the attempt record and the paper's text. The verifier agreed with all 31 outcomes. No finding is rated critical, so none was reviewed as one; it agreed with the ratings of all four findings (three minor, one none) and found that the weak clock checks in 10 sessions are not established as errors. In its section on text it also found that the README's six minutes for the claims on all 16 selections should be about four (230 s), and that cell 0's statement that the draft has the same asset count and size is shown by no output. Both are corrected: the README now says four, and the statement is removed. Still unavailable, it noted, are the paper's model code and the legends of Figures S1 and S2.

paper_notes.statement: The Methods do not say which sessions enter the analysis. Over all 153 sessions the selection gives about 35% more cells and 45% more recordings than the paper's 266 L2/3 cells from 78 recordings and 1075 L5 cells from 98; over the 104 sessions of the Sst-Cre and Vip-Cre Ai32 mice, whose units can be optotagged, every reading matches. No outcome here depends on the choice, but the counts do. Did the analysis use only those sessions?

The Methods take spontaneous activity from 'the period of mouse inactivity immediately following the task'. The dataset has a 10 s grey screen starting 18 to 29 s after the task and a 289 s spontaneous block about 940 s after it, and the mice run in most windows of both. Against the 10 s block alone L2/3 omission firing does not differ from spontaneous and L5 omission FSB is higher; against the 289 s block, or both, both are lower. Both blocks are adopted here. Which block, and which windows within it (all, or stationary only), did Figure 6 use?

How FSB is formed for a cell (spikes in bursts summed over windows, or a mean of per-window fractions), whether burst spikes must fall within the 250 ms window, and how cells without spikes in a condition are treated are not stated; the readings change the Figure 5C intercepts by a factor of about 1.7 and decide whether Figure 7A's L5 effect is significant. Which was used?

The selection of the 47 L2/3 and 658 L5 cells of Figures 7C and 7D is not stated. Requiring omission windows in both running states gives 365 and 1407 cells; requiring an omission spike in each state gives 210 and 1108. Under the first, L2/3 omission FSB is higher when running (p = 0.005) and both omission rate indices are positive. What rule gave 47 and 658 cells?

The model's code is not public, and the Methods do not give the L4 and L5 IT onsets relative to each other in Figures 2A and 2B, the conductance ranges of Figures 2 to 4, or the threshold that defines a burst or a positive error. With simultaneous onsets and the Methods' parameters, L4 below 12 nS with the prediction does not silence the neuron (0.9 spikes per run; without noise a release spike at 18.7 ms for L4 up to 10 nS and none from 12 nS, as basket inhibition at 1.2 times L4 outlasts L5 IT drive only from there), and at Low gain release spikes never occur (0 of 800 runs), so Figure 2A and 3C are not reproduced. Which onsets and ranges were used, and how is 'weaker than the predictive input' measured?

The Figure 5C legend prints the L5 slope as t(7523) = 8.1 with CI [-0.0011, -0.0007], a positive t with a negative interval, and the L2/3 slope as t(1860) = -0.59 with CI [-0.001, 0.004], whose centre is positive. The data here give a negative L5 slope (t = -2.91), as the Results and the CI have it.
The text of the preprint has a heading for Supplemental Figures with nothing under it, so the legends of Figures S1 and S2, which hold the tests of four findings, could not be read.

The degrees of freedom of Figure 7A and 7B, t(265) and t(1074), imply that all 266 L2/3 and 1075 L5 cells have Repetition 1 presentations both running and stationary. With the Methods' locomotion rule, 80% of active presentations are running and 26 of the 104 sessions of the Sst-Cre and Vip-Cre Ai32 mice have no stationary Repetition 1 presentation, so 67 L2/3 and 232 L5 cells cannot enter. How were running and stationary presentations defined for Figure 7, and how were cells without one of them treated?

entries.title: Chandelier-cell temporal gating and L5 bursting in mouse V1 (Jarzebowski & Bendor 2026)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Jarzebowski and Bendor (2026) on dandiset 000713, the Allen Institute's Visual Behavior Neuropixels recordings, which the paper reuses. It simulates the paper's two-compartment model of an L2/3 neuron from its Methods, and on the recordings selects putative pyramidal, image-responsive L2/3 and L5 units of VISp (layer from the CCFv3 annotation) and tests how their bursting and firing change with image repetition, omission, novelty and running.
